title: ISC U1·W4 — Data Management, Databases & the Data Life Cycle (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — data as the asset

Behind every system is data — and for a discipline named Information Systems and Controls, how data is structured, moved, governed, and protected is central. Meridian Building Group's job-cost, payroll, and billing data must be accurate, consistent, and available across systems. This week covers data governance, the relational database that organizes the data, the ETL and warehousing that move it for analysis, and the data life cycle that governs it from capture to destruction.

Data governance and data quality

Data governance assigns ownership and accountability for data — who defines it, who maintains it, and who may use it — and establishes a single source of truth so the same item means the same thing everywhere. Its goal is data quality, measured on dimensions including completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, timeliness, and uniqueness. Master data management (MDM) maintains consistent core entities (customers, vendors, items) across systems. Poor governance produces the duplicated, inconsistent data that corrupts every downstream report and analysis.

The relational database

Most business data lives in a relational database managed by a database management system (DBMS). Data is organized into tables (relations) of rows (records) and columns (fields). A primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key links a row to a related table, enforcing referential integrity (a job-cost record cannot reference a job that does not exist). Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. This structure lets one fact be stored once and related across the database — the efficiency and integrity that flat files lack.

Querying and integrity constraints

Data is retrieved and manipulated with SQL (Structured Query Language) — SELECT to query, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to change data — and the DBMS enforces integrity constraints: entity integrity (a non-null, unique primary key), referential integrity (valid foreign keys), and domain constraints (values within allowed ranges/types). These database-level controls complement the application input controls from Week 2: even if an application bug tries to write bad data, the database can reject a record that violates a constraint, protecting the integrity of the stored data.

Transactional versus analytical systems

Systems are tuned for different jobs. OLTP (online transaction processing) systems handle high volumes of day-to-day transactions — entering job costs, processing payroll — optimized for fast, reliable writes. OLAP (online analytical processing) systems support analysis and reporting over large historical datasets, optimized for complex reads. Running heavy analytics directly against the transactional system would slow operations, so data is typically copied to a separate analytical environment — which is where ETL and the data warehouse come in.

ETL, warehouses, and lakes

ETL — extract, transform, load — is the process of pulling data from source systems, transforming it (cleansing, standardizing, conforming), and loading it into a target for analysis. The target is often a data warehouse — an integrated, subject-oriented store of historical data — with smaller data marts serving specific functions. A data lake instead stores raw structured and unstructured data for flexible later use. The controls that matter here are the same as any data movement: reconciliation from source to target and validation that the transformation did not distort the data.

The data life cycle

Data is governed across a life cycle: capture/creation (with input controls), maintenance/storage (with access controls and backups), use (with authorization and logging), archival (retaining data no longer active but needed), and destruction/purging (securely disposing of data per retention policy). Each stage has its controls and its risks — a breach is most likely where data is stored or transmitted, and improper destruction can both leak information and violate retention requirements. Managing the whole life cycle, not just live data, is the discipline of data stewardship.

Data analytics and the controls connection

Governed, integrated data enables analytics — the descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analysis from BAR Unit 3 — and the ISC angle is that analytics are only as trustworthy as the data and the controls behind them. Continuous monitoring uses analytics over full populations to flag control exceptions in near real time. The discipline's throughline holds: well-governed data, structured in a sound database, moved through controlled ETL, and protected across its life cycle, is what makes both the financial statements and the analytics on top of them reliable.

Big data and emerging data architectures

Modern data extends beyond tidy relational tables. Big data is often described by the volume, velocity, and variety of information — including unstructured data (documents, images, sensor feeds) that relational databases handle poorly. NoSQL databases and data lakes store this flexible data, and cloud platforms provide the scale to process it. These architectures expand what analytics can do but raise the same governance questions in sharper form: where does the data come from, who owns it, is it accurate, and how is it secured? The technology changes; the data-governance obligations do not.

Data privacy and protection

Some data carries legal obligations. Personal and sensitive information is subject to privacy regulations that constrain how it is collected, used, shared, retained, and destroyed — the ISC discipline's privacy domain. Protecting it relies on the controls already covered (access control, encryption, life-cycle management) plus data classification (labeling data by sensitivity so the right controls apply) and data minimization (collecting and keeping only what is needed). A breach of regulated data brings both reputational and legal consequences, which is why privacy is governed as rigorously as financial-reporting integrity — the next unit develops it fully.

Backup, retention, and the integrity of the data store

Protecting the data store ties the data life cycle to operations. Backups and recovery procedures preserve data against loss or corruption; a retention schedule dictates how long each data type is kept to meet legal and business needs before secure destruction. Database controls — transaction logging, concurrency control so simultaneous updates do not collide, and checkpoints for recovery — preserve integrity within the DBMS itself. Emerging architectures add options: blockchain / distributed ledgers provide tamper-evident, append-only records useful where multiple parties need a shared, trusted history. Whatever the store, the objective is constant — data that is accurate, available, and protected across its whole life.

CMA bridge

The CMA program's dashboards and the auditor's data analytics both draw on MBG's database; ISC ensures that data is governed, normalized, and reconciled as it moves. The single-source-of-truth principle is exactly what lets the WIP figure in the finance report match the one in the operations system — data integrity is the foundation under every number.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply data governance + MDM for a single source of truth and data quality (completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, timeliness, uniqueness).
  2. Use the relational model: tables/rows/columns, primary and foreign keys, referential integrity, normalization, SQL, integrity constraints.
  3. Distinguish OLTP (transactions) from OLAP (analysis); move data via ETL into a warehouse/marts (or a data lake), reconciling source-to-target.
  4. Govern the data life cycle (capture → maintain → use → archive → destroy), each with its controls; enable trustworthy analytics and continuous monitoring.

Recap: data governance and master data management deliver a single source of truth and measurable data quality; the relational database structures data into keyed, normalized tables enforcing entity and referential integrity, queried with SQL; OLTP systems handle transactions while OLAP/analytics run on data moved through ETL into warehouses, marts, or lakes with source-to-target reconciliation; and the data life cycle — capture, maintain, use, archive, destroy — is governed with controls at each stage so the data underpinning the statements and the analytics stays reliable.

flashcards.back: Governance assigns data ownership/accountability for a single source of truth; master data management keeps core entities (customers, vendors, items) consistent across systems.
Completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity, timeliness, uniqueness.
Primary key uniquely identifies a row (entity integrity); foreign key links to another table (referential integrity — can't reference a record that doesn't exist).
Entity integrity (unique non-null PK), referential integrity (valid FKs), domain constraints (allowed values/types). Database-level controls beyond application input controls.
OLTP = high-volume day-to-day transaction processing (fast writes). OLAP = analytical processing over large historical data (complex reads). Separate them so analytics don't slow operations.
Extract from sources → Transform (cleanse/standardize/conform) → Load into a warehouse/mart. Control: reconcile source-to-target; validate the transformation.
Data warehouse: integrated, subject-oriented historical store (with data marts for functions). Data lake: raw structured + unstructured data for flexible later use.
Capture/create → maintain/store → use → archive → destroy/purge. Each stage has its own controls and risks (breach likeliest in storage/transmission; secure disposal per retention policy).

questions.q: A foreign key in a relational database enforces:
choices: Referential integrity (a valid link to another table)
questions.explain: A foreign key links to a primary key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

questions.q: Normalization of a relational database primarily:
choices: Reduces data redundancy and update anomalies
questions.explain: Normalization organizes tables to minimize redundancy and the anomalies it causes.
OLTP handles fast, reliable transaction writes; OLAP handles analytical reads.
ETL = Extract, Transform, Load; the transform step cleanses and conforms data.

questions.q: A key control over any data migration or ETL load is to:
questions.explain: Source-to-target reconciliation proves the data moved completely and accurately.
MDM maintains a consistent single version of core data entities across systems.

questions.q: Securely purging data at the end of its life cycle protects against:
questions.explain: Improper destruction can leak sensitive data and breach retention requirements.
